records.title: Why can't I dig deeper than about a hand?
records.summary: A hard, cemented iron-rich layer lies close under the surface, typical of laterite. Hand tools will not break a solid one, so work with the shallow soil.

records.title: Can I break the hard layer?
records.summary: Only loose, gravelly spots can be scraped out a little. A solid sheet cannot be broken by hand; build raised beds or containers above it instead of losing days and tools.

records.title: Is this soil dead?
records.summary: No. It is poor, shallow and probably acidic, but the grass tufts and thorny shrubs show life is possible. Organic matter, mulch and the right crops bring it back slowly.

records.title: Why is the soil red?
records.summary: Iron is left behind after heavy rains wash much of the rest away over a very long time. Red usually means old, leached soil with few nutrients.

records.title: Why does rain run off instead of soaking in?

records.title: What should I build first?
records.summary: Choose a safe spot, then catch water: on a gentle slope, a low stone line across the main runoff path with a safe spill point, plus a few pits or one raised bed.

records.title: How do I know where to put stone lines?
records.summary: Watch runoff in a rain or pour a little water to see which way it runs. Lay a low, level line across that direction. On flat ground where water pools, do not build lines that trap water.

records.title: How high should stone lines be?
records.summary: Start low, about ankle to shin high, and raise them only after watching how water moves. Always leave a safe overflow; never block a natural watercourse or build a dam.

records.title: How do I keep water for dry spells?
records.summary: Use clean, covered household containers fed from a roof or sheet, and thick mulch on the soil. Never use a planting pit as a pond: roots drown in water that cannot drain.

records.title: How many pits should I start with?

records.title: What goes in the bottom of a pit?

records.title: Where do I get soil to fill pits and beds?
records.summary: From fine soil collected behind stone lines, gaps between stones, dry stream-bed silt, rotted leaf litter and old empty termite mounds. Leave out stony crumbs and anything that smells of chemicals.

records.title: My bed fills with water and stays full. Why?
records.summary: The hard layer is stopping drainage. Stop sending water there, raise the bed, and cut a stable overflow notch that leads to a safe place.

records.title: What do I do if the soil seems acidic?
records.summary: Treat the fizz check as a rough clue only. Grow tolerant crops and add compost. If you try clean ash or crushed shell, use a small, well-mixed trial only, and never set the amount by the fizz.

records.title: How do I make compost?
records.summary: Layer dry brown material and green material with a handful of soil between layers, keep it as damp as a wrung-out cloth, and turn it now and then. It is ready when dark, crumbly and earthy-smelling, usually after a couple of months in warm weather.

records.title: When do I plant?
records.summary: After repeated soaking rains, not one shower, when the soil is moist down to the hard layer. Choose crops whose time to maturity plus a two-to-three-week buffer fits the wet weeks left.

records.title: The rain came before I was ready. What now?
records.summary: Start small: make one stable bed or a few pits where water drains, fill them with soil and compost, and sow a fast crop after the next soaking rain. Finish other works after watching the runoff.

records.title: How long until the first food?
records.summary: Amaranth greens in about four to six weeks, cowpea in roughly two to three months, millets in about three months, groundnut in three to four months. Cassava, pigeon pea and trees take far longer.

records.title: Is the hard layer good for anything?
